rows.answer: The human brain contains roughly 86 billion neurons [1]. This figure was measured in 2009 by dissolving brains into a uniform soup of cell nuclei and counting samples [1].
Glial cells are about as numerous as neurons, not ten times more numerous as older textbooks claimed [1].

An action potential is an all-or-nothing event, meaning a neuron either fires a full spike or none at all [1]. Because of this, stimulus strength is coded by how frequently a neuron fires and how many neurons fire, rather than by the size of individual spikes [1].

Myelin acts as a fatty insulating sheath that allows signals to jump between gaps in the sheath known as nodes of Ranvier [1]. This process is called saltatory conduction, enabling myelinated axons to conduct signals at up to about 120 metres per second [1].
GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter, which makes the receiving neuron less likely to fire [1].
Most of the brain's energy is used to pump ions back across membranes after neurons signal, which restores the gradients for future action potentials [1].
A burst of high-frequency stimulation in a rabbit's hippocampus made the synapse respond more strongly for hours afterwards [1]. This effect is known as long-term potentiation, or LTP [1].

The NMDA receptor acts as a coincidence detector that opens when both the sending and receiving cells are active at the same time [1]. It is a glutamate receptor involved in long-term potentiation [1].

Patient H.M. was still able to learn new motor skills, such as getting better at tracing a star in a mirror over several days [1]. However, he could no longer form new long-term memories of facts or events [1].

A confident memory can still be wrong because recalling a consolidated memory makes it unstable and subject to being updated or distorted during reconsolidation [1]. Similarly, emotional flashbulb memories can be very vivid rather than reliably accurate [2].
A full cycle through the sleep stages takes about 90 minutes [1]. A typical night contains four to six of these cycles [1].

Caffeine keeps people alert mainly by blocking adenosine receptors in the brain [1]. Adenosine is a by-product of energy use that accumulates during wakefulness and contributes to sleep pressure [1]. By blocking these receptors, coffee prevents adenosine from promoting sleepiness [1].
A small region of the hypothalamus called the suprachiasmatic nucleus sets the circadian clock that times sleep [1].

Sleep strengthens and stabilizes memories formed during the day by transferring them to the cortex [1]. During sleep, cerebrospinal fluid flows through the brain via the glymphatic system to wash out waste products like beta-amyloid [2]. Additionally, sleep allows the brain to clear accumulated adenosine and helps restore attention, reaction times, and mood regulation [3][5].
During sleep, the space between brain cells expands by about 60 percent [1]. This expansion allows cerebrospinal fluid to flow through the brain tissue and wash out waste products [1].
Yes, one study found that after 17 to 19 hours without sleep, performance on certain tasks was as poor as having a blood alcohol concentration of 0.05 percent [1].

When an expected reward is withheld, dopamine neurons briefly fall silent at the exact moment the reward should have arrived [1]. This dip in activity represents a reward prediction error indicating that the outcome was worse than expected [1].

Popular writing often calls dopamine the pleasure chemical, but research suggests this label is misleading [1]. Instead of driving pleasure, dopamine appears to drive the motivation to pursue a reward, or "wanting" [1]. Pleasure itself actually depends on small hotspots that use opioid and related signalling [1].

Drugs like cocaine are addictive because they raise dopamine levels directly, which bypasses the brain's prediction machinery [1]. As a result, the brain receives a false signal that the experience was better than expected every single time [1]. This causes cues linked to the drug to acquire a powerful pull, and with repeated use, the desire or "wanting" for the drug can grow even as the actual pleasure or "liking" fades [1].

In Parkinson's disease, tremor is a main symptom caused by the gradual death of dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra [1]. These specific neurons feed circuits in the basal ganglia that help start and scale movement [1]. Symptoms like tremor usually only appear after a large fraction of these neurons has been lost [1].
The dopamine signal resembles temporal difference learning, an algorithm from machine learning [1]. This connection links neuroscience and artificial intelligence closely [1].

Emotional experiences are remembered better because arousing events cause the body to release stress hormones, and noradrenaline acts in the amygdala to boost memory storage in the hippocampus and cortex [1]. This phenomenon results in vivid flashbulb memories, such as recalling where you were during shocking news [1].

In 1848, a railway worker named Phineas Gage survived an accident where an iron tamping rod passed through his skull and destroyed much of his left frontal lobe [1]. Contemporary accounts describe him as having become impulsive and unreliable, though later reports exaggerated the change and noted he partly recovered [1]. His case provided an early clue that the frontal lobes shape personality and self-control [1].

Emotion is actually a working part of good judgment rather than its enemy [1]. Bodily feelings tied to past outcomes guide our choices, and people with brain damage affecting these emotional signals tend to make disastrous decisions [1]. Therefore, emotion helps good decisions [1].
The prefrontal systems that exert control keep maturing well into the twenties, often cited as around age 25 [1].

Animals learn that a sound predicts danger through fear conditioning, where a tone is sounded just before a mild shock is administered [1]. After a few pairings of the tone and the shock, the tone alone is enough to trigger responses like a racing heart and freezing [1]. Joseph LeDoux and other researchers traced this specific learning process to changes occurring within the amygdala [1].
When people cannot rehearse or group items, the real capacity of working memory is closer to about four chunks [1]. A chunk is a unit of meaning, meaning capacity ultimately depends on knowledge [1].

The invisible gorilla experiment showed that attention acts as a powerful filter, allowing people to miss things in plain view when they are focused on another task [1]. This phenomenon is known as inattentional blindness [1].

For tasks that require thought, the brain does not truly perform two things at once [1]. What feels like multitasking is actually a rapid switching between different tasks [1]. Each switch comes with a cost because the brain must reconfigure its rules and goals [1].

When you daydream, a specific set of brain regions known as the default mode network becomes active [1]. This network is also active during mind-wandering, remembering the past, imagining the future, and thinking about yourself and others [1].

Yes, driving a London taxi is linked to changes in the brain's posterior hippocampus, a region involved in spatial memory [1]. A study found that this region was larger in taxi drivers than in control subjects, with its size correlating with the years spent driving [1]. Furthermore, a study tracking trainees showed that those who successfully qualified experienced growth in this area over the training period [1].

When one eye of a kitten was kept closed during an early window, the visual cortex rewired to favor the open eye [1]. As a result, vision through the deprived eye remained poor even after it was eventually opened [1].

Whether adult humans grow new neurons is genuinely debated, as two 2018 studies reached opposite conclusions [1]. One study reported that new neuron production in the human hippocampus drops to undetectable levels in adulthood, while the other reported it continues into old age [1]. Differences in tissue handling and methods likely contribute to this disagreement, leaving the question open [1].

Stroke patients can regain the use of a weak arm through constraint-induced movement therapy [1]. This therapy restrains the healthy arm, forcing the patient to use the weakened arm intensively [1]. This intensive use drives reorganization in the motor cortex and can improve function years after the stroke [1].

A child's brain removes unused connections to make the remaining circuits more efficient [1]. This removal follows a use-it-or-lose-it principle, where active connections are kept and strengthened while rarely used ones are eliminated [1].

You cannot tickle yourself because your brain predicts the sensory consequences of your own movements using a copy of the motor command. This prediction causes the self-produced touch to be cancelled, making it feel less intense than an outside touch [1].

Predictive coding is a framework in neuroscience stating that the brain constantly generates predictions about incoming sensory signals rather than passively waiting for them [1]. In this process, predictions are sent down the processing hierarchy and compared with incoming signals, with only the resulting mismatches travelling upwards to update the brain's model of the world [1]. What we experience through this framework is the brain's best guess regarding the causes of its sensory input [1].

The inside of a mask looks like a normal face pointing outwards because the brain has a strong expectation that faces are convex, which overrides the depth cues [1]. This illusion demonstrates the brain's predictions at work [1].

A sugar pill can reduce reported pain through the placebo effect, which occurs because believing a treatment will work can change what we feel [1]. Brain imaging shows that this belief leads to measurable changes in pain-related activity alongside the reported reduction in pain [1]. This happens because perception blends predictions with sensory input, meaning expectations can change our actual experience [1].

In 1973, Tim Bliss and Terje Lømo provided the first direct evidence for Hebb's learning theory by showing that a burst of high-frequency stimulation in a rabbit's hippocampus strengthened a synapse for hours afterward [1]. This phenomenon is known as long-term potentiation, or LTP [1].

In the 1990s, Wolfram Schultz recorded dopamine neurons in monkeys that received drops of juice to study dopamine and reward [1]. When juice arrived unexpectedly, the neurons fired a burst, but once monkeys learned a light predicted the juice, the burst moved to the light [1]. When the expected juice was withheld after the light appeared, the neurons briefly fell silent [1].
Nelson Cowan summarized work in 2001 indicating that when people cannot rehearse or group items, the real capacity of working memory is closer to about four chunks. [1]

London taxi drivers must memorise thousands of streets to pass an exam known as the Knowledge [1]. In a 2000 study by Eleanor Maguire and colleagues, it was reported that the posterior hippocampus of these taxi drivers was larger than that of control subjects [1]. Additionally, the size of this brain region correlated with the number of years spent driving a taxi [1].

Marcus Raichle and his colleagues described a pattern of brain regions that becomes more active when people rest quietly with no task, naming it the default mode network in 2001 [1]. This network is active during activities such as mind-wandering, daydreaming, remembering the past, imagining the future, and thinking about oneself and other people [1].

Rajesh Rao and Dana Ballard published an influential computational version of the predictive processing framework in 1999 [1]. This framework suggests the brain constantly generates predictions about sensory input and compares them with incoming signals [1].

James McGaugh showed that blocking the signaling of stress hormones like adrenaline and noradrenaline weakens the memory advantage for emotional material [1]. This mechanism involves noradrenaline acting in the amygdala during arousing events to boost memory storage in the hippocampus and cortex [1].

Rats with almost completely depleted dopamine still showed normal facial expressions of liking when sugar was placed in their mouths, but they would not work to obtain it [1]. Dopamine therefore drives the motivation to pursue a reward rather than the pleasure of receiving it [1]. Pleasure itself relies instead on small hotspots that use opioid and related signaling [1].

David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel shared the 1981 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their work on the visual system [1]. Their research demonstrated critical periods of plasticity, showing that depriving a kitten's eye of vision early in life rewires the visual cortex, whereas the same deprivation affects adult cats very little [1].

Nodes of Ranvier are gaps in the myelin sheath that allow signals to jump between them during saltatory conduction [1]. This process enables myelinated axons to conduct signals at speeds of up to about 120 meters per second [1].

In the Iowa gambling task, healthy players learn to avoid risky decks and exhibit stress responses prior to choosing them [1]. Conversely, patients with damage to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex do not show these stress responses and make disastrous choices [1].

During slow-wave sleep, the hippocampus replays recent experiences in compressed bursts known as sharp-wave ripples [1]. These ripples are coordinated with slow oscillations and sleep spindles in the cortex to help transfer and stabilize memories [1].
